newsitem.title: USA: Iraq threatened U.S. jets before attacks - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Iraq threatened U.S. jets before attacks - Pentagon.

text.p: The Pentagon said on Friday an investigation had determined that Iraqi radar threatened two U.S. F-16 jets before they fired missiles at anti-aircraft sites in southern Iraq last Saturday and Monday.

"Further analysis of the Nov. 2 and 4 missile launches by U.S. aircraft over Iraq has confirmed that both F-16CJ aircraft encountered threat radar emitters," the Defence Department said in a statement, praising what it called "highly professional" performances by both pilots.
Defence officials said the day after the first incident that there was some indication Iraqi ground radar had not threatened the F-16 before the pilot fired a missile.

But further investigation showed that neither pilot was mistaken in firing "Harm" high-speed anti-radiation missiles at the ground sites, the Pentagon said on Friday. It was not known if either missile hit the mark.

Iraq denied that either event occurred and accused the United States of "groundless fabrication" in what it called a political ploy on behalf of President Bill Clinton before he was re-elected this week.

The Pentagon said on Friday that "the assessment team also found the performance of the pilots to be highly professional and that they operated properly under rules of engagement," which allow them to fire when threatened.

After repeated warnings from Washington, Iraq earlier promised not to threaten U.S. and allied pilots patrolling "no-fly" zones over southern and northern Iraq, established after the Gulf War to restrict Iraqi military activity.

Defence Secretary William Perry said this week that both incidents occurred south of the 32nd parallel within 25 miles 40 km of each other and that the southern zone had been quiet for at least a week before the shooting, with no indication Iraq had stepped up activity against the jets.

The United States expanded the southern no-fly zone northward from the 32nd to the 33rd parallel, up to the outskirts of Baghdad, in September after Iraq's President Saddam Hussein sent troops into northern Iraq to back one Kurdish faction against another.
Washington also responded to the incursion by attacking southern Iraq with 44 ship- and air-launched cruise missiles.
